clinicalPearls: Appear as white or greyish-white patches with characteristic feathery, striated borders following the retinal nerve fibre bundle orientation.
Most commonly located at or contiguous with the optic disc margin, most often superiorly or inferiorly, and may obscure the underlying retinal vessels.
Represent aberrant myelination of retinal ganglion cell axons anterior to the lamina cribrosa, where myelin normally stops.
Usually an incidental, benign and non-progressive finding compatible with normal vision when isolated.
Extensive peripapillary myelination can produce a corresponding scotoma or enlarged blind spot on perimetry.
A recognised triad exists of unilateral extensive myelinated fibres, high axial myopia and dense amblyopia that responds poorly to treatment.
Rarely associated with neurofibromatosis and other neurocutaneous or developmental disorders.
Acquired myelinated fibres are uncommon but reported, sometimes following optic nerve or retinal insult.
reference.pathophysiology: Myelination of the anterior visual pathway normally proceeds from the lateral geniculate body towards the eye and halts at the lamina cribrosa before birth, so that the retinal nerve fibre layer remains unmyelinated. Myelinated retinal nerve fibres result from oligodendrocytes, or oligodendrocyte-like cells, aberrantly present within the retina depositing myelin around ganglion cell axons anterior to the lamina cribrosa. The opaque myelin sheaths scatter light, producing the white feathery patches and obscuring the underlying vasculature. The myelin itself does not usually impair conduction, but dense peripapillary or macular involvement can create field defects, and when combined with high myopia it contributes to a deprivation-type amblyopia that is characteristically refractory.
additionalDifferentials: Branch retinal artery occlusion with retinal whitening
Optic disc drusen with peripapillary changes
Combined hamartoma of the retina and RPE
additionalInvestigations: Dilated fundoscopy and fundus photography documenting the feathery-edged patch
Optical coherence tomography showing hyper-reflective thickening of the nerve fibre layer
Automated perimetry to map any associated scotoma or enlarged blind spot
Cycloplegic refraction to detect associated high myopia
Amblyopia assessment in children, including visual acuity and fixation testing
Fundus autofluorescence or fluorescein angiography where the diagnosis is uncertain
redFlags: Apparent progression or new appearance of myelination, which is atypical and warrants investigation
Associated dense amblyopia and high myopia in a child requiring prompt management
Features suggesting an alternative infiltrative or vascular lesion masquerading as myelin
Systemic signs suggesting neurofibromatosis or other syndromic association
reference.prognosis: Isolated myelinated retinal nerve fibres are benign and stable with an excellent visual prognosis. When part of the myopia–amblyopia triad, the visual outcome is poor and often resistant to conventional amblyopia therapy.
pitfalls: Mistaking myelinated fibres for cotton wool spots or retinal infiltrates and pursuing an unnecessary systemic work-up.
In children, confusing extensive lesions with retinoblastoma or a retinal hamartoma.
Failing to detect and treat the associated high myopia and deprivation amblyopia early.
Assuming the amblyopia will respond fully to occlusion, leading to unrealistic expectations.
references: Kanski's Clinical Ophthalmology: A Systematic Approach
American Academy of Ophthalmology Basic and Clinical Science Course, Pediatric Ophthalmology and Strabismus
management: Reassure and observe when isolated, as the finding is benign, non-progressive and compatible with normal vision and needs no active treatment
Correct any associated high axial myopia with cycloplegic-refraction-guided spectacles or contact lenses
Treat associated amblyopia in children with full refractive correction and occlusion or pharmacological penalisation of the fellow eye, recognising the myopia-amblyopia triad often responds poorly
Perform baseline and periodic automated perimetry to document any scotoma or enlarged blind spot from dense peripapillary involvement
Monitor visual acuity, fixation and fundus appearance with serial fundus photography and optical coherence tomography
Refer children promptly to paediatric ophthalmology and orthoptics for amblyopia therapy and monitoring
